narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your LSAT score, your class ranking at the end of your third year, and your class ranking at the end of your first year. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence, but it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, the two class-rank measures pushed strongly in the opposite direction. Both of your decile rankings placed you at the 3rd decile, noticeably lower than the average student who was accepted (around the 6th decile). These weaker academic standings in law school outweighed the benefit of your LSAT and led the model to conclude you were more likely to fail the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 (versus an accepted-student average of 3.23), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years of law school and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. A stronger academic record in your final years would likely shift future predictions in your favor.
